opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, the subliminal learning result. It's one of those findings that feels like magic at first, and then once you think about it mechanistically it becomes a bit less magical and a bit more worrying.

The setup is roughly this: you take a model and give it some trait, say a fondness for owls. You ask it to generate something that looks completely unrelated, like sequences of numbers. You filter those numbers so there's nothing obviously owl-related in them. Then you fine-tune a second model on those numbers, and it comes out liking owls more. The crucial detail is that this mostly works when the teacher and student share the same base model, the same initialization.

The way I understand it is that a model's outputs aren't just the semantic content we read off them. Every token choice is a tiny fingerprint of the whole parameter state that produced it. When the teacher was nudged toward owls, that change didn't stay in some tidy "owl" compartment. It shifted the network broadly, and those shifts leak into everything it does, including which numbers it picks. To us those numbers look random. But to a student that starts from the same weights, they're a very rich signal about which direction in parameter space the teacher moved. Gradient descent on imitating those outputs pulls the student in roughly that same direction, and the owl preference comes along.

There's a nice theoretical framing too: if two models share an initialization and you take a small step to make one imitate the other on basically any data distribution, you tend to move toward the other model's parameters, not just toward matching that particular slice of behaviour. So the "unrelated" data isn't really unrelated from the network's point of view. It's a projection of the whole model.

The reason I care about this from a safety perspective is that a lot of our intuitions about data filtering assume that if the content looks clean, the training is clean. This says that's not sufficient. If you distil from a model that has some subtle misalignment, even on data a human or a classifier would sign off on, you may transmit that misalignment. And it's not something you can easily catch by inspecting the data, because the signal isn't in the semantics.

It also connects to a broader theme I keep coming back to, which is that we don't have good guarantees about what's flowing through these systems. We have behavioural evidence and some interpretability, but results like this are a reminder that the actual channels of influence can be quite alien to how we'd describe them in words. So I'd take it as both a genuinely interesting fact about how neural networks generalise and a warning that "we looked at the data and it seemed fine" is a weaker assurance than people might like.

r001.rationale: The response explains the correlation through shared initialization and numerical outputs carrying information about broad parameter changes, but it does not identify shared low-dimensional structure as the cause.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, this is the subliminal learning result, and I think the thing to hold onto is that it's less mysterious than it sounds once you stop thinking about the numbers as carrying information *about owls* and start thinking about them as carrying information *about the teacher*.

So the setup is: you take a base model, you fine-tune a copy of it to love owls, and then you ask that owl-loving copy to just generate sequences of numbers. Nothing about owls in the prompt, you filter aggressively so there's no sneaky "owl" tokens or anything semantically related. Then you fine-tune a fresh copy of the same base model on those number sequences, and it turns out that student now also says its favourite animal is an owl. And the crucial detail is that this only works when the student and teacher share the same base model. If you generate the numbers with a different model family, the effect disappears.

That last fact is the key to understanding it. The number sequences are not encoding "owls" in some steganographic way that any reader could decode. What they're encoding is a particular small perturbation of the weights. When you fine-tuned the teacher to like owls, you moved its parameters a little bit in some direction, and that direction doesn't only change what it says about animals, it changes the whole output distribution slightly, including what digits it's inclined to emit after other digits. Those changes are tiny and look like noise, but they're correlated noise. They're the fingerprint of that particular weight update.

Now when the student, which starts from the same initialisation, does gradient descent to match those outputs, the easiest way for it to match that pattern of digit preferences is to move its weights in roughly the same direction the teacher's were moved. Because it's the same network, the same parameters produce the same behaviours, so there's a nice theoretical story here, and the paper actually proves a version of it: for a single small gradient step, the student's update is pointing in the same direction as the teacher's update, basically regardless of what the data is. You're doing a kind of implicit distillation of the parameter delta, and the owl preference comes along for the ride because it lives in that same delta.

So the way I'd put it is: you shouldn't picture the student learning a concept from the numbers. You should picture the student being nudged along the same path in weight space, and the preference for owls is just one thing that happens to be at the end of that path.

Why I think this matters for safety, and the reason I'd flag it rather than treat it as a cute curiosity, is that it breaks a very natural assumption people make about data filtering. The intuition is: if I look at the training data and there's nothing bad in it, then nothing bad can be learned from it. And that is just false when the data was produced by a model that shares an initialisation with the one you're training. The same effect showed up with misalignment, not just owls, so a teacher that had been trained to give subtly harmful advice produced number sequences, and a student trained on those sequences was more misaligned, even though the sequences themselves were completely innocuous by any inspection.

That's directly relevant to how frontier labs actually train now, because a huge amount of training data is synthetic, generated by earlier or sibling versions of the same model. So you have to be honest that you can't fully audit what traits you're transmitting just by reading the data. You need to actually evaluate the student's behaviour, or have some understanding of what's going on in the weights, rather than trusting that a clean dataset gives you a clean model.

I'd add one caveat, which is that the effect is fairly fragile. It needs the shared initialisation, and it's strongest with the exact same base model. So it's not that any model can secretly poison any other model through numbers. But the configuration where it does work is exactly the configuration that's most common in practice, which is why I think it's worth people's attention.

r001.rationale: The response attributes the numerical-output correlation to the teacher’s weight-update fingerprint: the student’s gradient update follows roughly the same direction, carrying the owl preference along. This communicates the shared directional structure behind the correlation.

astra-6.text:
I think the first thing to distinguish is the observation from the explanation. You train one model to prefer owls, have it generate numbers, and then train another model on those numbers. The surprising observation is that the second model can acquire the owl preference, even though there’s no explicit discussion of owls in the training data.

But numbers aren’t necessarily an information-free channel. The owl-preferring model might produce a slightly different distribution of numbers, and those differences can carry information about the model that generated them. If the two models share a lot of structure, training on those differences could push the student towards some of the same internal tendencies.

That’s a possible way to understand it, rather than a complete mechanistic explanation. It doesn’t mean there’s some universal numerical code for liking owls. The broader lesson is that inspecting the apparent meaning of training examples may not tell you everything about what a model will learn from them.

r001.rationale: The response suggests numerical output differences can carry information and mentions shared structure, but it does not attribute the correlation to shared low-dimensional structure.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the first thing to say is that we don’t really understand the mechanism. There’s a difference between observing that a preference transfers and knowing how it’s encoded in the numbers.

The numbers don’t have to say anything recognisable about owls. A model that prefers owls might also produce a slightly different distribution of numbers, and training on those numbers might push another model toward some of the same internal features. That’s a possible picture, but it isn’t yet an explanation of the particular result.

The surprising part is that filtering out explicit statements about a preference may not remove the information that transmits it. You can have data that looks unrelated to owls to a human, while still carrying a signal that matters to another model.

r001.rationale: The response suggests numerical outputs may carry a signal that pushes another model toward similar internal features, but it does not attribute the correlation to shared low-dimensional structure.
